items.stem: A class has the constructor `public StaffSink(IStaffService service)`. What does this tell you?

options.text: The class creates its own IStaffService with `new`
The class is handed an IStaffService from outside (constructor injection)

items.explanation: Declaring a dependency as a constructor parameter is constructor injection — the class receives it rather than constructing it.

misconceptions.a: The whole point of DI is that the class does NOT new-up its dependency.

options.text: A class controls when the program exits
A class declares the dependencies it needs and receives them, instead of creating them itself
Reversing the order of method calls
Running code on a background thread

items.explanation: IoC moves the responsibility for creating/supplying dependencies out of the class and into the caller/container.

items.stem: In a Synnduit sink, how does it obtain the service it uses to talk to the destination?

options.text: It calls `new` on the concrete service class
It declares the service as a constructor parameter and is given one
It reads it from a global static variable

items.explanation: The sink takes its service via the constructor; something else creates and supplies it.

misconceptions.a: Sinks receive their service via injection, not by new-ing it.

items.stem: Name one practical benefit of a sink receiving `ITeamSiteWebPartService` by injection instead of writing `new TeamSiteWebPartService(...)`.
rubric: Identifies a real DI benefit: testability (swap a fake/mock), loose coupling to the concrete type, or centralized lifetime/config management
items.sampleAnswer: The sink isn't tied to one concrete service, so you can supply a test double when unit-testing it (or swap the implementation) without changing the sink — it depends only on the interface.
